cards.title: WACC: the hurdle every investment must clear
cards.body:
A company's weighted average cost of capital is the blended return its investors require: what shareholders and lenders each expect, weighted by how much of the capital they provide. It's the discount rate in a DCF and the bar new projects must clear to create value.

The formula is WACC = E/V × cost of equity + D/V × cost of debt × (1 − tax rate). Debt is cheaper for two reasons: lenders get paid first, and interest is tax-deductible. The cost of equity is usually estimated with CAPM: the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium.

The insight that matters on the buy side: growth only creates value when return on invested capital exceeds WACC. Growth below WACC destroys value, however exciting it looks.
cards.example: Capital is 70% equity at 9% and 30% debt at 5%, with Ontario's 26.5% combined corporate tax rate. WACC = 0.7 × 9% + 0.3 × 5% × (1 − 0.265) = 6.3% + 1.1% ≈ 7.4%.
cards.takeaway: Growth creates value only when returns on capital beat WACC.

cards.title: Protein: how much actually builds muscle
cards.body:
For lifters, the best-supported target is around 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. A widely cited 2018 meta-analysis found that extra muscle gains from protein plateaued around that intake on average, with some people benefiting from up to about 2.2 g/kg.

Spreading it over three to five meals of roughly 0.3 to 0.4 g/kg each tends to work better than one giant serving. For vegetarians, quality matters a bit more: many plant proteins contain less leucine, the amino acid that most strongly switches on muscle building, so eat slightly larger portions and combine sources like soy, legumes, grains, eggs and dairy.

Total daily intake matters most. Timing is a refinement, not a requirement.
cards.example: At 75 kg, aim for about 120 g a day. That could be 40 g overnight oats at breakfast, a 35 g tofu bowl at lunch, a 30 g lentil dinner and a 20 g Greek yogurt snack.
cards.takeaway: Hit about 1.6 g/kg a day, spread over a few meals.

cards.title: The FHSA: the best tax deal for a first home
cards.body:
Launched in 2023, the First Home Savings Account combines the best parts of the RRSP and TFSA. Contributions are tax-deductible like an RRSP, and qualifying withdrawals to buy a first home are tax-free like a TFSA. Few accounts give you both.

You can contribute $8,000 a year, up to $40,000 lifetime. Unused room carries forward, but only up to $8,000, so the most you can add in one year is $16,000. Crucially, room only starts building once you open the account, which makes opening one early, even empty, a smart move.

If you never buy a home, the balance can move to your RRSP without using RRSP room. And you don't have to claim the deduction right away; you can save it for a higher-income year.
cards.example: Open an FHSA in 2026, even with nothing in it, and you get $8,000 of room for 2026. Contribute nothing, and in 2027 you'd have $16,000 available. Wait until 2027 to open it and you'd have only $8,000.
cards.takeaway: Open an FHSA early: room only starts accruing once the account exists.

cards.title: Hume's guillotine: you can't get ought from is
cards.body:
In 1739, David Hume noticed a sleight of hand in moral arguments. Writers would describe how things are, page after page, then suddenly shift to how things ought to be, without explaining how one followed from the other.

His point, now called the is-ought problem or Hume's guillotine, is that facts alone never logically produce a value judgment. To reach a conclusion about what should happen, you need at least one premise about what matters: fairness, welfare, liberty, growth.

This is a powerful tool in economics and policy debates, where empirical findings are often presented as if they settled moral questions. When someone argues from data to a prescription, look for the hidden value premise. Often the real disagreement lives there, not in the numbers.
cards.example: A study finds a carbon tax cuts emissions at a modest cost to GDP. That's an is. Concluding that governments should adopt one requires an ought, such as we should cut emissions when the cost is low. Debate the premise, not just the study.
cards.takeaway: Facts alone never prove what should be done; find the hidden value premise.

cards.title: Learn the notes on the low E string
cards.body:
Plenty of guitarists play songs for years without knowing where the notes are. Fix that one string at a time, starting with the low E, because that's where the roots of barre chords and power chords live.

The musical alphabet runs A to G, and almost every pair of neighbouring natural notes is two frets apart. The exceptions are B to C and E to F, which are only one fret apart. That's all you need. On the low E string, the natural notes fall at: E open, F 1, G 3, A 5, B 7, C 8, D 10, and E again at 12. At the 12th fret everything repeats an octave higher.

Sharps and flats sit in the gaps, like F sharp at fret 2. Learn the naturals first, then fill in the rest.
cards.example: Drill: say a random note out loud, find it on the low E as fast as you can, and play it. Two minutes a day for a week. Then play an E-shape barre chord on each one: G at 3, A at 5, C at 8.
cards.takeaway: Natural notes are two frets apart, except B to C and E to F.

cards.title: The Lindy effect: old ideas tend to last
cards.body:
For things that don't age biologically, like books, ideas, technologies and institutions, every year of survival tends to predict more years ahead. That's the Lindy effect, named after Lindy's deli in New York, where comedians in the 1960s joked that a show's future run was proportional to how long it had already lasted.

Nassim Taleb popularized the idea in Antifragile. A book that has stayed in print for 100 years has passed a century of filtering; last month's bestseller hasn't been tested at all. The same logic applies to investing principles, training methods and recipes.

It isn't a law, just a useful prior when you face too many options and too little information about which ones will matter.
cards.example: Choosing what to read this year? Pair every new release with something that's been in print for at least 50 years. Marcus Aurelius has been read for nearly 2,000 years; that's a strong signal.
cards.takeaway: If something has lasted a long time, expect it to keep lasting.

quiz.question: Why is debt usually cheaper than equity in a WACC calculation?
options: Banks are required to lend at low rates
Debt never has to be repaid
Lenders are paid first and interest is tax-deductible
quiz.explanation: Lower risk for lenders plus the interest tax shield make after-tax debt cheaper than equity.

quiz.question: Roughly how much protein per day should a 70 kg lifter aim for?
Which statement about the FHSA is true?
options: Contribution room only starts building once you open the account
Withdrawals for a first home are taxed as income
You can contribute $40,000 in a single year
quiz.explanation: Unlike the TFSA, FHSA room doesn't accrue from age 18; it starts the year you open the account.

quiz.question: Someone says: unemployment fell after the policy, so we must expand it. What would Hume point out?
options: A value premise is needed to get from the fact to the prescription
quiz.explanation: Even if the fact is true, should-claims need a premise about what we value, like lower unemployment being worth the cost.

quiz.question: On the low E string, which fret is C?
quiz.explanation: B is at fret 7, and B to C is just one fret, so C is at fret 8.

quiz.question: According to the Lindy effect, which is likely to remain in print longer?
options: A book in print for 80 years
quiz.explanation: For non-perishable things, a long track record of survival predicts more survival.
